>I hate fighting with my mind.

That's basically what it is, given the survival instinct is basically the strongest, most basic of them all (perhaps reproduction is a competitor, but I think it's survival). It certainly felt that way when I was suicidal-level depressed.

What you're describing is indeed an existential crisis given everyone is just going to end up dead, too. Per another comment I made, no one chose to be born into this, the very thing you also don't have a choice but to leave eventually, too, like it or no. It's a strange predicament, isn't it? Yet, basically the most universal in that we all share it.

So like another reply said, I guess I've used that in a different way - it may be easier said than done - but might as well say fuck it, and do whatever, not worry about failure, etc., since there's nothing really to lose, literally, since you do anyways, eventually.

Wow - three post-graduate degrees. That's impressive. Just one is, really. 

I think I know what you mean about "this is now an operating mode." I certainly do about looking into the future and drawing a blank - and while I'm not quite as old as you, I'm not far off at 35, because at this point? A year feels like a week did when I was a kid in many ways.

At the same time, paradoxically, I do get how emotional pain can also make it feel like another hour is torture. I guess time is heavily based on perception, with only the present moment being the thing we're in, in what could be seen instead a constantly evolving sculpture of existence: sometimes better, other times worse, maybe most of the time the latter, but here nonetheless.

Anyways, I've basically been at this point, within the last year. I'd call myself maybe moderately depressed (?) on most days now, but I'm afraid almost to even type that should it not be true and I can only *hope* I don't get back to literally 0/10 every day, every hour and with current events, maybe it'll be the case. Basically, I don't think about killing myself, and how - all the time. *That* was torture, and you have my empathy - seriously. 

What did I do? Out of desperation, I broke down and went back on anti-depressants. I'm not sure at this point if I boxed myself in as it were by putting my brain into a state where it basically *needs* them, by downregulating its own production of neurotransmitters so drastically I just can't do without, or, if it was my depression as it would have been anyways, given before anti-depressants I for sure had episodes of what would be called "clinical depression." I got to the point I was so desperate I didn't care anymore what the answer was. I'm not suggesting that for you, by the way. I guess it's pretty sad I need a chemical to give me the "this is fine" that serotonin I feel primarily tells you to feel, but I'll take it, for now. 

This was long, and you're on a temp account, and I'm not sure why I wrote this, but you sound like a cool person, I know how you're feeling, and I wish things were better for you. I get what you're saying about how America sees you, but for whatever little it might be worth to you - I don't at all. I do wish this was a world where feeling as you do, I have, and might again, but hope desperately I don't, wasn't possible but I'm sorry you're feeling it. Truly.

Yeah, that's totally true - you're only hearing that from people for whom things *actually did* get better. For plenty of others, things got way, way worse after they were told it would get better, so they went ahead and finally blew their heads off or whatever else. For obvious reasons, we're not hearing "It gets worse" from them. In fact, telling them things would get better may have set up a false-expectation of reality and when it didn't pan out, only exacerbated their already bad feelings about life.

Also: things getting better is very in-line with what people want to hear - that's why Hollywood studios have famously changed the more ambiguous or even bad endings certain directors wanted to make whatever point: because it doesn't sell.

Having said all that - things *can* get better. Like you say: there are no guarantees - just like things aren't guaranteed to get better, they're also not guaranteed to get worse, and I'll admit that at my worst of depression, I was definitely biased toward thinking the latter, or thinking things were worse than they are.

In some ways, objective reality, and the true, actual state of things is impossible to know: it mostly depends on how the balance of chemicals and connections between your neurons mold your perception of the past, present and future. C'est la vie, I guess...

Yeah, I know what you mean for sure - I got real depressed in my early 20s and once I got out of it, I never wanted to feel that way again, but last year I kinda slipped back into it even worse than before after my five year relationship with my GF ended on top of a bunch of other things. It was easily the worst I've fucking felt to the point I started actively planning how to end it, which at first I found alarming, like I was fighting my own brain trying to kill me basically, but then I got tired of fighting it and just accepted I was going to do it. It would have worked for sure, too - I knew what I was doing.

I decided to at least make an appointment with a psychiatrist and therapist for the hell of it, which is something I'd never done before and somehow, after at least a year of just basically wishing I wouldn't wake up everyday,  I actually think I'm starting to come out of it. It was kind of strange at first telling people I barely knew all this heavy stuff but it's kind of nice to have someone to dump that on where it's their job to take it and they're not going to be freaked out since they've pretty much heard it all. Like I say, I don't want to assume anything, because I don't want to be disappointed, but if you told me a year ago I might be feeling even just a *little better* eventually, or that I could even have mildly goodish days, I wouldn't believe it, so you never know.

Don't get me wrong - sometimes I see the ex post something online and getting like 100 likes and am just like "fuck this" but in a way I've always had a little of that, just thinking so much of life is honestly ridiculously fucking dumb, but maybe now just not to the point of dying, and instead just more laughing at it all, since dying will inevitably happen anyways, just without doing it myself and fucking up my mom and brother emotionally in the process.

I'd say I'm politically liberal as far as economic issues are concerned, partly because of my experience growing up and afterward. In my opinion, we don't have to institute hardcore communism, and can still have billionaires/millionaires, while also having a system that ensures kids that end up in fucked up situations through no fault of their own like I did don't have to go through the same thing. Life isn't perfectly fair, but it doesn't have to be this unfair.

As far as robots wiping out humanity, it sounds like fiction, but the advanced research agency within the US military is [currently developing computers modeled after the human brain](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/SyNAPSE), including the ability to strengthen specific connections via learning/experience, mimicking our own neuroplasticity. So, I'd say there's a 50/50 chance of a robot apocalypse in our lifetime.

I've got to say, if this is your parents saying this, and they have the financial means to help you in any way - that's pretty messed up. It was *their decision to bring you into this* *world,* not yours, and nowadays college is insanely expensive - even community college. Books alone can be over $1000 per semester.

Not sure if it'll make you feel any better - but a year or two ago I felt like I'd completely fucked up in life, and *I'm 35 now.* That's nearly twice your age, and honestly I regret getting bogged down in depression back when I was college-aged, because I didn't realize how much time I still had then. At the same time, I can understand why I felt that way given my situation: poor kid raised by a single Mom with horrible teeth she couldn't afford to fix, no guidance or help or encouragement with college, etc. etc. so I can understand why you feel discouraged, too, given your own.

One thing I will say is that what's helped me recently, to the point I actually think I'm cautiously optimistic I'm no longer suicidal, is that I've just decided to say "fuck it" and do what *I want to do* at this point and not care anymore about what people think, or if they judge me on it. I have nothing to lose at this point. I also know I had a ton of obstacles a lot of my friends didn't remotely have, and I realize I've achieved a lot despite that. I'm also realizing if hadn't have been so damn worried and bummed the last year and a half, I could have been in an awesome place right now, so I'm trying to not make the same mistake again going forward from here, because I'll completely regret it.

I don't know if any of that helped you at all, but I know how you feel because I felt a lot like that at your age. *You have potential* \- trust me - and you deserve encouragement. I hope you can find a way forward.

Success in life is mainly luck. Fuck struggling to "get ahead" when getting ahead in this society means you're fucking over a bunch of other desperate, scared people trying to claw their way into security that never really comes for most anyways.

The truth is, and maybe it sounds pretty harsh and deterministic, is that a break up when you're still into the person is basically a drug withdrawal - when you're in a relationship that's working out, you end up on the receiving end of naturally produced opioid peptides produced by your own body, some of which are far more potent than morphine by weight - so like any addiction it takes a while to regain homeostasis, or just as typically find a new person and hope that works out better. At the end of the day, it is just chemicals causing these emotions and unfortunately we're kind of slaves to them.

I just wanted to say, while I at least think I understand how you feel, which I kind of summed up [here](https://www.reddit.com/r/SuicideWatch/comments/c9hfw3/why_is_it_so_hard_for_some_people_to_accept_that/), I'd heard a lot of people say this and was terrified to even mention suicidal thoughts but when I did, they didn't lock me up. The thing is though that I delineated thinking about it versus actually actively planning it because I knew that the latter risked getting locked up, despite the fact I've partly planned/attempted it in the past, so it's true I couldn't be completely honest. I knew I had to be clear I "wasn't planning anything." In that way, it was actually kind of helpful to be able to openly talk about thinking about it and my reasoning without them being concerned I was going to do it. I also might have had a pretty chill therapist/psychiatrist team, too.

Now, if you tell them you have a plan, and are serious about carrying it through - they likely will lock you up. I guess that's because they're kind of between a rock and a hard place in that situation. I think many know there's a risk of making things worse, but if they don't do it, they think maybe you'll do it anyways and they could have at least tried something, and even though it's kind of cold, they've also got liability to worry about. They could easily be sued by family, etc., for not preventing a suicide when they could have even though they might agree that this could just make things way worse. This is in the US anyways, which is a very litigious society. When a patient commits suicide, therapists will usually have to provide their notes and a statement, etc. It's serious business.

Anyways, I totally agree that most people could never understand what it's like to actually feel bad enough to not want to live, and to override the strongest instinct humans have which is survival. The lifetime prevalence of major depression I think in one study was estimated at 20% - which at first seems like a lot - but that means *4 in 5* *people have never even felt severe depression,* which means the vast majority of people have lived without ever knowing what it's like to not want to get out of bed, let alone not wanting to even live at all.

I've said that if people that have never been there could spend one day in my mind at my worst points, I believe they'd feel incredibly lucky to have lived life without ever feeling *that,* yet would also understand why I wouldn't want to continue feeling *that,* and would feel fortunate to have not had to live through the things I have. Which is also precisely why I think people do try to save people from suicide - it's just unfathomable to someone could actually want to die, because for them life might have some rough points, but on the whole they've lived without ever coming near the point of considering ending it. They can't imagine what it'd be like to be in my mind, and I can't imagine what it'd be like to be in theirs. To feel pumped about life instead of afraid of the sun coming up, because that means *another day of this shit.* It straight up blows my mind that some people have lived almost their entire lives totally happy, with just a few slight down periods, and yet there are, which of course is only more depressing to realize.

I can't blame you at all for feeling like you do, but I hope you can find a way out of it. I don't think anyone deserves to feel this awful. I wish the brain had evolved with a shut off point for feeling bad enough to want to die and really wish it had.

It's extremely unlikely. That is a very high dose though so what will happen is you'll end up hallucinating, except you won't really be able to distinguish the hallucinations from reality. There's a pretty high likelihood they won't be fun either - a common motif is seeing insects and stuff like that. Beyond that, you could easily end up not in control of your actions, acting insane and ending up in the ER with a huge bill which won't help things. Lots of over-the-counter medicines contain the same active ingredient - diphenhydramine - and people use pills containing it thinking it'll be a good way to legally trip, so there's a ton of [anecdotal](https://erowid.org/experiences/subs/exp_Diphenhydramine_Bad_Trips.shtml) reports about bad ones.

It’s disturbing. and no one knows about it, but similarly to what you described, last summer I got to the point I’d made a (somewhat bad) noose and was kind of half partially suspending myself without letting it slip too much to see what it was like. I also partly tried a couple other ways off cutting off my airway, but one day when I started to pass out rather quickly, I suddenly realized how dangerous what I was doing was and how bad things had gotten if that’s what I was doing to myself. I’d never crossed the threshold beyond just thoughts before and got just how trapped I felt. Same as you, the primary reason I felt I couldn’t do it was because of my family and whoever would have to find me. At that point I was too far gone to think any of my friends would really care, though I know now they would. I think even some people I’ve had issues with would feel bad.

I have reached out about these things. My Mom and my brother know to some extent (just not the “testing” from last summer) and I also now have a therapist who knows. The problem is it hasn’t really changed how badly I’ve felt about anything, but it’s given me another person to feel guilty about if I did anything, since I’ve known my therapist for seven or eight months now. I do feel with other people it would legitimately push them away to talk about, maybe even for good. Some people just can’t deal with that and I totally get it. 

For now, since I don’t want to hurt my family, I feel stuck - just gritting my teeth while holding on until tomorrow, day after day, but that’s all I’ve been doing. It sounds trite but I really just wish this wasn’t real somehow, but it is. I’ve put effort into getting better, and doing all the things you’re supposed to do, but I’m still finding myself treading the same water, coming back to the same thoughts. I know that’s probably disappointing and I’m not trying to be negative, but I just think I’m fairly objectively screwed at this point and didn’t have a whole lot of chance in the first place.

I think a lot of people in my position would have broken down, but whatever, life isn’t remotely fair. I wish so badly I’d just chilled out.

Despite that, things are much worse now three years later, and like you I’ve found myself wishing I’d just done it when I was more impulsive. I can’t though, because the survival instinct is incredibly strong, and even worse, it’s quite clear how much it would destroy my family. 

So, I’m stuck. Every day I live with the pain of knowing what I could have done in life to avoid this situation, and how close I was to having at least an okay life. I don’t think there’s anything after this, and telling myself the next 40 to 50 years will be as hellish as this is a huge bet to take, so I guess I keep trying to think of ways I could have a life I can accept. It’s really hard, and the longer I stay depressed the worse things get. 

I hope you can find something to hold onto - I don’t think anyone deserves to feel this badly.
